# Joshua 11: research notes

**A note on what I found:** The verse-by-verse material is good. Most of it comes from Guzik (enduringword.com), Precept Austin, and the older writers collected on Bible Hub and StudyLight. I found no pages where a church tradition sets out its own official view of this chapter. I didn't reach seedbed.com, lcms.org, 1517.org, ag.org, desiringgod.org or gty.org before I ran out of searches. In section 2, I compare individual older commentators instead. The pages I read don't say which tradition each writer belongs to, so I've left that out. I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. One warning: the Bible Hub "Study Bible" and "Questions" notes have no named author.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- The northern kings heard about Israel's wins in the south and joined forces. The size of their army shows they thought Israel had to be stopped now or they would be conquered. Guzik draws a lesson: when believers commit themselves to God, they may face more opposition. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/
- "Jabin" was probably a royal title passed down in Hazor, like "Pharaoh" in Egypt (Howard, quoted by Guzik). George Bush says the name means "wise" or "intelligent," and that the later Jabin of Judges 4 had the same name. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary
- The word "heard" ties chapters 9–11 together. The Gibeonites heard and made peace; the southern and northern kings heard and went to war (Mathews, quoted on Precept Austin). Barber says Hazor was the largest city in Palestine, with perhaps 40,000 people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary

**vv. 2–3**
- Precept Austin's geography notes: Chinneroth (from a word for "harp") is the Old Testament name for the Sea of Galilee. The "lowland" means the low hills near the coast, here the part north of Mount Carmel. Dor was about 47 miles southwest of Hazor, on the coast. Jabin sent messengers across the whole north. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary
- "Mizpah" means "watchtower." Several towns had that name; this one lay at the foot of Mount Hermon (Madvig). Howard notes this alliance was broader, more scattered and more dangerous than the five kings of chapter 10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/

**v. 4**
- Guzik sees two new difficulties: a huge army and better weapons. Hess calls "horses and chariots" the most feared war machinery of the day. Guzik adds that each challenge in Joshua is bigger than the last, and the Christian life can be like that. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/

**v. 5**
- Precept Austin calls this the Canaanites' last attempt to destroy God's people, and probably the largest force Joshua faced. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik: God would not say "do not be afraid" unless fear was a real problem. Joshua needed a fresh promise for a bigger challenge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/
- Barber's argument: Merom was upwards of 70 miles from Gilgal, so Joshua had likely already marched north before the Lord spoke to reassure him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary
- Calvin also says Joshua went on the attack, deep into enemy country, before God's promise took away any fear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-11.html
- Matthew Henry's points: God fits our trials to our strength, and destroying the horses and chariots showed Joshua's self-denial. Things the heart leans on can harm faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary
- Precept Austin: Israel was not to keep the horses or chariots for an advantage, but to stay dependent on Yahweh. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary

**v. 7**
- Joshua used boldness and strategy, attacking by surprise (Clarke). Howard notes that "all the people of war" is a phrase found only in Joshua and seems to stress the nation's unity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/

**v. 8**
- Guzik thinks this may have been the biggest battle of the conquest, yet there was no obvious miracle. God worked in ordinary ways, and Boice thought it was probably the bloodiest battle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/
- Clarke repeats an old story recorded by Procopius: Canaanites who fled to Sidon supposedly went on to found Tangier in North Africa. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/

**v. 9**
- Joshua obeyed exactly. Madvig says crippling the horses showed contempt for modern weapons, because Israel's trust was to be in God alone (Psalm 20:7). Guzik applies this to Christians who use "the devil's tools." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/

**vv. 10–11**
- Hess says Hazor's size and its place in ancient records support the phrase "head of all these kingdoms." Guzik argues that God judged a guilty society as a whole, as with the Flood, Sodom, and later Israel and Judah. He adds that children dying does not mean their souls were lost. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/
- Guzik's summary: Hazor was one of only three cities burned in the conquest (with Jericho and Ai), and archaeology confirms it was destroyed in the late fourteenth century B.C. and not rebuilt until Solomon's time. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/ (Bible Odyssey gives a different date; see v. 11 in section 3.)

**v. 12**
- Gill: Joshua was not acting out of revenge, cruelty or greed. He was obeying God's command given through Moses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/11-12.htm
- George Bush: "Utterly destroyed" refers to the people; many of the cities themselves, and their spoils, were preserved. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary

**v. 13**
- "On their mounds" can also be translated "on their hills." Bush's note says cities on high ground could be held easily, so it made sense to keep them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary

**v. 14**
- Bush says Israel took the plunder with the exception of such things as had been employed for idolatrous purposes (Deuteronomy 7:25). https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary

**v. 15**
- "Commanded" appears three times for emphasis. Joshua was a doer of the word and not only a hearer (James 1:22). The Believer's Study Bible says the destruction was not their idea but God's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary

**vv. 16–17**
- Guzik explains the regions: the central highlands, the southern desert, Goshen, the lowland, the Jordan valley, and the coastal plains. Madvig says "took this entire land" means control of the region, not the capture of every city. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/

**v. 18**
- George Bush: "a long time" is literally "many days." Comparing chapter 14, he thinks at least six or seven years, the first occupied in the south and the remaining five or six in the north. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary
- Guzik says the slow conquest fit God's plan to give the land "little by little" and gave Canaanites time to repent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/
- Alan Carr takes Joshua's long fight as a lesson in determination for Christians. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary

**v. 19**
- Precept Austin: Only one made peace and that one did it deceptively. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary
- Matthew Henry: other cities could have made peace if they had humbled themselves, but they never asked for terms. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/11-20.html

**v. 20** (the most discussed verse; see section 2)
- Guzik: hardening means God hands people over to the sin already in their hearts (Romans 1:24–28). Truly repentant Canaanites like Rahab were accepted. What could not be accepted was a grudging surrender with no real turning to God. Madvig: "God hardened the Canaanites' hearts, not to keep them from repenting, but to prevent them from surrendering to Israel in unrepentance." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/
- Ellicott translates the phrase as "strengthen their heart," meaning made them stubborn. He says this shows the conquest of Canaan was not intended to be a massacre of the unresisting inhabitants. https://biblehub.com/joshua/11-20.htm

**vv. 21–22**
- Howard: the account of the Anakim is unusually harsh and thorough because of how much they had frightened Israel. Guzik: God saved the hardest enemy for last, after training Israel through months of battle. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-11/
- These were the giants the spies feared in Numbers 13. Some Anakim remained in the coastal cities later held by the Philistines. https://www.preceptaustin.org/joshua-11-commentary
- Keil & Delitzsch: Gaza and Ashdod were given to Judah but never actually occupied. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/11-23.htm

**v. 23**
- Several older writers say "the whole land" does not mean every place. Poole says it means the greatest and best part. Barnes says many districts were not yet subdued (Joshua 13:1–6). The Pulpit Commentary says the complete extermination of the Canaanites formed no part of his commission or his plan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/11-23.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: God had said he would drive the Canaanites out little by little (Exodus 23:28–30). Israel's later failures came from their unfaithfulness, not from Joshua's work being incomplete. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/11-23.htm
- Matthew Henry: the war ended in peace from the Canaanites, not peace with them. He sees it as a picture of the believer's coming rest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/11-23.htm
- Calvin: some of the land given out by lot was not conquered until long after Joshua died. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/joshua-11.html

## 2. Where writers really differ

**v. 20: how does God harden hearts?** I found three different answers.
- **God arranged it.** Keil & Delitzsch say God ordered things so that the Canaanites hardened their hearts. They deny that God would have spared them if they had welcomed Israel. Following Augustine, they say the verse explains why Israel was not tempted into more of the mercy it wrongly showed Gibeon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/11-20.htm
- **God left them to their own sin.** Clarke says God left them to their own stubbornness and pride after they had sinned against the light they had. The Pulpit Commentary says their free will was not interfered with, and it doubts that Canaanites who came asking for peace would all have been killed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/11-20.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/11-20.htm
- **Both together.** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the words mean more than God merely permitting it. Matthew Henry says Pharaoh and the Canaanites hardened themselves first, and then God's judgment hardened them further. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-11.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/11-20.html
- **Could they have been saved?** F. B. Meyer says God loved them as He loves the world. They were included in the propitiation of Christ. They might have been saved, as Rahab was. Adeney says God hardens a heart only after a person has sinned, and that hardening is not a cause of sin but a fruit of it. https://biblehub.com/sermons/joshua/11-20.htm
- Kelly takes a harder line. He denies that the Canaanites were offered a real choice to flee or make peace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/11-20.html

**vv. 11–14: should "no one who breathed" be read literally?**
- A bible.org article reports Copan's view. Words like "utterly destroy" were standard war language that meant total victory, not wiping out every person. The same article also presents the opposite view: that the conquest was God's capital punishment on a whole nation. https://bible.org/article/canaanites-genocide-or-judgment
- An unsigned Bible Hub note says the wording stresses defeat of organised resistance, since pockets of Canaanites still appear later (Joshua 13:13). https://biblehub.com/joshua/11-20.htm

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- **v. 10:** Excavations by Yadin and Ben-Tor found a fortified Canaanite city of about 200 acres. This fits Hazor's leading role in v. 10. The buildings were destroyed by fire during the 13th century B.C.E. Interpretations differ regarding the precise date of the 13th-century destruction and its perpetrators. https://ar.bibleodyssey.org/articles/hazor/
- **v. 11:** Ann Killebrew says Joshua may have destroyed Hazor, but so could Egypt, the Sea Peoples, or a rival Canaanite city. She still does not think Joshua can be ruled out. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/video-gallery/the-destruction-of-hazor/ Another Bible Odyssey video says Hazor is one of the few places where archaeology seems to support Joshua, unlike Jericho. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/video-gallery/archaeology-and-conquest/
- Bible Odyssey also notes that the book of Joshua gives two different accounts of whether the whole land was conquered (compare vv. 16–23 with chapter 13). https://bibleodyssey.org/people/main-articles/joshua

**Catholic**
- **vv. 20–23:** A Catholic Answers episode cites the historian van Wees, who thinks the claimed total destruction was largely fictional and points to differences with Judges. It then turns to Origen. Origen read v. 20 spiritually: the Canaanites stand for the sins Christians must wipe out completely. Gregory adds that God may leave a few small faults in us, like Canaanites still living in the land. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/did-god-command-genocide-in-the-old-testament

**Not found:** anything from Orthodox sources (oca.org), the NET Bible notes, or teachers of prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace on this chapter.

**Dating conflict to note in your commentary:** Guzik (citing Madvig) dates Hazor's destruction to the late 1300s B.C. Bible Odyssey's archaeologists put it in the 1200s and say the date is still debated.
